claims.text: The degree of local chemical short-range order governs premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Chemical short-range order arises from differences in atomic stress, electronegativity, atomic volume, and charge among constituent elements.
Higher chemical short-range order produces a more stable local atomic environment.
Higher short-range order raises the energy barrier for surface-atom mobility and thereby delays premelting.
As-synthesized CrMnFeCoNi or similar HEA nanoparticles have a near-random atomic arrangement with varying degrees of short-range order.
Slow cooling from elevated temperature enhances short-range order relative to rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching retains a more random atomic distribution.
Chemical short-range order can be quantified using atom-probe tomography or high-resolution X-ray diffraction to assess atomic-stress or charge-distribution variations.
The interplay of positive and negative atomic stresses balances the local atomic environment.
Short-range-ordered regions have a more uniform, lower-energy environment that resists surface disordering.
Low-short-range-order regions have less balanced interactions and a lower barrier to surface-atom mobility.
Enhanced-short-range-order nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than quenched, more random nanoparticles.
Enhanced-short-range-order nanoparticles will exhibit a sharper transition to the molten state.
Enhanced-short-range-order nanoparticles will show less surface diffusion or liquid-like surface-layer formation across the tested temperature range.
The quenched, near-random control will have lower thermal stability and earlier premelting.
The proposed relationship applies to HEA nanoparticles containing at least four principal elements.
The proposed relationship is most valid from approximately 600 K through the nanoparticle melting regime.
The quantitative effect of short-range order on premelting temperature may vary with alloy composition and nanoparticle size.
